lessons.name: Airbus CabinMarker
lessons.summary: Airbus CabinMarker is a four-kilogram robot that marks aircraft seat positions, reducing repetitive floor-level work for assembly operators.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Airbus CabinMarker is a four-kilogram robot that marks aircraft seat positions, reducing repetitive floor-level work for assembly operators.

![Close-up of the compact CabinMarker robot on an aircraft floor](/img/lessons/robots_robot-airbus-cabinmarker.webp)
*Close-up of the compact CabinMarker robot on an aircraft floor. Source: [Airbus](https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/stories/2026-06-meet-the-versatile-airbus-robot-automating-aircraft-seat-installation), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A narrow task can be valuable:** Airbus targets the bending, kneeling, and crawling involved in marking seat positions, rather than replacing an entire assembly team.
- **The reported time saving is concrete:** 150 minutes becomes 30 minutes; subtracting gives 120 minutes saved for the described task, not the whole aircraft build.
- **Ergonomics means fitting work to people:** less floor-level marking can protect workers' backs and knees while they retain responsibility for the wider process.

> **Key idea:** Automating one awkward, repeatable operation can matter more than giving a robot a general-purpose body.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A mobile base carries a marking pen:** the small wheeled machine moves through an unfinished cabin to mark where seats belong.
- **CAD supplies the layout:** computer-aided design files describe the aircraft configuration; ASSEMBLY reports that these files program the marking operation.
- **Think of a physical printer:** a digital layout becomes marks on a real surface, rather than pixels on a screen.
- **Tool changes remain proposals:** Airbus describes camera-based corrosion scouting and rail cleaning/taping as future applications, not established capabilities.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L["CAD layout"] --> R["Robot marking path"]
  R --> M["Seat bolt marks"]
  M --> H["Human seat fitting"]
```

| Specification | Reported value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass | 4 kg |
| Manual task time | 150 minutes |
| Robot task time | 30 minutes |
| Industrial certification | December 2025 |
| Rollout planned in June 2026 | 2 units, Toulouse A321 line, late 2026 |

## Key terms

- **CAD**: software used to describe a designed object's geometry and layout.
- **Industrialisation**: turning a prototype into equipment suitable for repeatable production use.
- **End effector**: the task-performing tool, here the marking pen.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the marking demonstration:** distinguish the robot's marks from the later human work of actually fitting seats.
2. **Recalculate the time comparison:** divide 150 by 30 to obtain a fivefold reduction in task duration.
3. **Sketch a paper-only analogue:** convert a simple seat layout into ordered marking coordinates; buying access to Airbus's internal machine is not required.

## Used in

- **Airbus** developed CabinMarker in-house; its June 2026 article planned A321XLR deployment for late 2026, while ASSEMBLY reported use in August.
- **Rollout reports differ:** neither article establishes the current deployment status; keep the June plan separate from later reporting.
- **Student access and price are unknown:** treat this as an industrial case study, not a publicly documented kit or SDK.

lessons.name: AmphiBot
lessons.summary: AmphiBot is EPFL’s family of snake-like amphibious research robots, using coordinated body waves to investigate crawling, swimming, and biologically inspired control.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

AmphiBot is EPFL’s family of snake-like amphibious research robots, using coordinated body waves to investigate crawling, swimming, and biologically inspired control.

![AmphiBot III with a long chain of connected body segments](/img/lessons/robots_robot-amphibot.webp)
*AmphiBot III with a long chain of connected body segments. Source: [EPFL BioRob](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/biorob/research/amphibious/amphibot/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Locomotion need not mean wheels or legs:** a chain of bending segments can move through water and, with suitable ground contact, crawl.
- **A small controller can coordinate many joints:** the AmphiBot II paper generates movement onboard instead of streaming every bend from an external computer.
- **Keep generations separate:** the photograph shows AmphiBot III; the numerical specifications below describe the seven-joint AmphiBot II documented in 2006.

> **Key idea:** Coordinated timing between neighbouring joints can turn simple repeated bends into whole-body movement.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Each powered segment contains a motor, battery, and controller:** connected waterproof elements form the body, with a separate head.
- **A central pattern generator creates rhythms:** coupled oscillators, or interacting repeating signals, generate a wave travelling along the body.
- **Think of synchronised software timers:** each timer repeats, but neighbouring timers have deliberate delays rather than firing together.
- **Parameters shape motion:** frequency sets repetition rate, amplitude sets bend size, and wavelength describes how far a body wave extends.
- **Ground contact changes:** AmphiBot II uses passive wheels for directional friction when crawling; researchers remove those wheels for swimming.
- **Swimming tests used an air tube:** a small pump maintained internal pressure to help prevent water leaks; waterproof housings did not mean unrestricted underwater operation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Rhythm parameters"] --> O["Coupled oscillators"]
  O --> J["Joint bends"]
  J --> W["Travelling body wave"]
  W --> M["Crawl or swim"]
```

| AmphiBot II specification | Paper's value |
| --- | --- |
| Powered joints | 7 |
| Overall length | 77.2 cm |
| Element length | 9.4 cm |
| Element cross-section | 5.5 × 3.7 cm |
| Battery per element | 600 mAh |
| Battery endurance per element | Approximately 2 hours in normal conditions |

## Key terms

- **Amphibious**: able to operate both on land and in water.
- **Oscillator**: a system producing a repeating signal.
- **Phase offset**: the timing difference between repeating signals.
- **Passive wheel**: an unpowered wheel turned by contact with the ground.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the swimming race:** follow one bend from head toward tail, rather than tracking only the robot's forward movement.
2. **Make a free plotting exercise:** draw seven sine waves with successive phase offsets; this illustrates coordination, not EPFL's complete oscillator equations.
3. **Try aligned versus delayed waves:** compare zero phase offsets with a quarter-cycle delay between neighbours, then describe which plot resembles travelling motion.
4. **Read the historical paper:** research-platform purchase access and current price are unknown; no hardware is needed for the plotting exercise.

## Used in

- **EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory (BioRob)** uses AmphiBot to study locomotion controllers and biological hypotheses; its project page also connects later development to Envirobot.

lessons.name: ARA620 UHP Sprayer
lessons.summary: ARA620 UHP Sprayer is Ecorobotix’s tractor-mounted implement that recognises individual plants and applies tightly targeted sprays instead of treating an entire surface.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

ARA620 UHP Sprayer is Ecorobotix’s tractor-mounted implement that recognises individual plants and applies tightly targeted sprays instead of treating an entire surface.

![Ecorobotix ARA sprayer working behind a tractor in a field](/img/lessons/robots_robot-ara620.webp)
*Ecorobotix ARA sprayer working behind a tractor in a field. Source: [Ecorobotix](https://ecorobotix.com/crop-care/ara-620-uhp-sprayer/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Computer vision changes physical treatment:** identifying a crop or weed matters only if the correct nozzle sprays the correct patch of ground.
- **It is an implement, not a self-driving tractor:** the tractor provides movement; ARA supplies plant recognition and targeted application.
- **Savings depend on the field:** Ecorobotix advertises up to 95% less plant-protection product, explicitly depending on weed density; this is not a universal guarantee.

> **Key idea:** A plant classifier becomes useful machinery only when its decisions arrive at the right place and time.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Six camera modules observe plants:** RGB cameras capture colour, while 3D cameras provide depth information for the recognition system.
- **A spray bar carries individually targeted outlets:** its height adjusts automatically, and black protective covers help limit spray drift.
- **A tablet selects crop and treatment:** the operator configures the application rather than writing recognition code in the field.
- **Think of an event-processing pipeline:** observations trigger treatment actions as the tractor moves; classification and delivery cannot be designed independently.
- **A timing example:** the advertised 7.2 km/h equals 2 m/s; a hypothetical 0.1-second delay would correspond to 20 cm of travel, not measured ARA latency.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Plant images"] --> D["Crop or weed decision"]
  D --> N["Select spray nozzles"]
  N --> S["Treat target patch"]
```

| ARA620 S G2 specification | Manufacturer's value |
| --- | --- |
| Working width | Up to 6.20 m |
| Ground speed | Up to 7.2 km/h |
| Productivity | Up to 4 ha/hour |
| Spray nozzles | 156, spaced 4 cm apart |
| Target spray patch | 6 × 6 cm |
| Water / mixture tanks | 600 L / 300 L |

## Key terms

- **Nozzle**: the outlet shaping and directing a spray.
- **RGB**: red, green, and blue colour image channels.
- **Spray drift**: droplets moving away from the intended treatment area.
- **Hectare**: an area of 10,000 square metres.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the Ecorobotix presentation:** identify which parts belong to the tractor and which belong to ARA.
2. **Reproduce the timing calculation:** convert kilometres per hour to metres per second, then multiply speed by delay.
3. **Inspect the official assembly views:** locate the six vision boxes and three spray booms; commercial price and student access are unknown.

> **Watch out:** Agricultural chemicals require the machine's operating precautions and the product's label instructions; do not prototype chemical spraying as a classroom exercise.

## Used in

- **Ecorobotix** applies this plant-by-plant approach to crop care; it is a useful perception-to-actuation case study, not a public robot-learning development kit.

lessons.name: BDX droids
lessons.summary: BDX droids are Disney’s expressive two-legged robotic characters, combining human puppeteering with learned balance and artist-authored motion.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

BDX droids are Disney’s expressive two-legged robotic characters, combining human puppeteering with learned balance and artist-authored motion.

![Three Disney BDX robotic characters with large heads and two articulated legs](/img/lessons/robots_robot-bdx-droids.webp)
*Three Disney BDX robotic characters with large heads and two articulated legs. Source: [Disney Research](https://la.disneyresearch.com/publication/design-and-control-of-a-bipedal-robotic-character/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Personality is an engineering requirement:** a head tilt or distinctive walk must remain recognisable while the machine stays upright.
- **Animation is not enough:** a screen character cannot fall onto a visitor, but a real robot must respect balance and contact with the floor.
- **Human direction remains important:** Disney describes a puppeteer shaping the performance; lifelike behaviour does not imply independent conversation or general intelligence.

> **Key idea:** The operator chooses the performance while a learned controller makes expressive movement physically executable.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Articulated legs provide mobility:** the large head supplies expressive poses, with lights and sound contributing to the show.
- **Animators author desired motions:** reinforcement learning trains a controller in simulation to imitate those motions while handling physical disturbances.
- **An animation engine blends commands:** the runtime combines operator input and animation sources, rather than playing one immutable recording.
- **Think of a game engine with physics:** the puppeteer supplies intent, while the controller continually resolves how the body can actually move.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Artist motions"] --> T["Simulation training"]
  T --> P["Learned policy"]
  H["Puppeteer commands"] --> E["Animation engine"]
  E --> P
  P --> M["Joint motion"]
```

| Published platform detail | Value or role |
| --- | --- |
| Support legs | 2 |
| Neck-and-head degrees of freedom | 4 |
| Degrees of freedom per leg | 5 |
| Training environment | Simulation |
| Performance direction | Human puppeteering |

- **A joint-count example:** two five-degree-of-freedom legs plus the four-degree-of-freedom neck-and-head assembly give 14 primary motion coordinates, excluding show functions such as actuated antennas.

## Key terms

- **Degree of freedom**: one independently variable coordinate of a mechanism's motion.
- **Reinforcement learning**: training through rewards for behaviour during repeated trials.
- **Policy**: the controller mapping observations and commands to actions.
- **Sim-to-real**: transferring behaviour developed in simulation onto physical hardware.

## Getting started

1. **Watch Disney's research video:** separate the operator's high-level choices from the small continuous corrections needed for balance.
2. **Annotate a short performance:** record head direction, stepping, and sound as separate tracks; this is a free observation exercise, not robot access.
3. **Read the pipeline figure:** trace animation authoring through simulated training to live control, noting where the puppeteer enters.
4. **Plan around access limits:** public purchase price and a student hardware-access route are unknown; the paper is a study resource, not an assembly manual.

## Used in

- **Disney Research Zurich** connects this platform to character animation and robot learning; Disney reports appearances at events and park playtests, not industrial manipulation tasks.

lessons.name: Colossus
lessons.summary: Colossus is Shark Robotics’ remotely operated tracked firefighting robot, carrying interchangeable tools into hazardous places while firefighters direct it from a distance.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Colossus is Shark Robotics’ remotely operated tracked firefighting robot, carrying interchangeable tools into hazardous places while firefighters direct it from a distance.

![Colossus spraying foam during a firefighting mission at an industrial site](/img/lessons/robots_robot-colossus.webp)
*Colossus spraying foam during a firefighting mission at an industrial site. Source: [Shark Robotics](https://www.shark-robotics.com/colossus-firefighting-robot/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Teleoperation can be the right product:** the firefighter makes decisions while the machine carries the hose and takes the exposure to heat and debris.
- **The user interface matters:** camera views and remote tool controls are part of the rescue system, not optional extras around the drivetrain.
- **A real deployment grounds the lesson:** Colossus supported the Paris Fire Brigade during the Notre-Dame fire on 15 April 2019.

> **Key idea:** Keeping judgement with a human can still move the dangerous physical work away from that human.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Tracks move the platform:** two electric motors drive a low, broad vehicle that carries mission equipment rather than resembling a human firefighter.
- **Modules change the task:** options include a water cannon, equipment basket, stretcher support, and video turret with thermal imaging.
- **Cameras return observations:** the operator steers and directs tools using visual information, including heat-sensitive images when the appropriate module is fitted.
- **Think of a remote client-server session:** commands travel out and observations travel back; the operator remains part of the control loop.
- **A flow-rate example:** at the technical table's 3,000 litres/minute, dividing by 60 gives 50 litres/second; that describes water delivery, not an onboard tank capacity.
- **The vendor page is inconsistent:** its FAQ also claims 3,800 L/min; this lesson uses the technical table, not a verified maximum for every configuration.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H["Human operator"] --> C["Radio commands"]
  C --> R["Tracks and mission tool"]
  R --> V["Camera observations"]
  V --> H
```

| Manufacturer's technical table | Listed value |
| --- | --- |
| Gross weight | 525 kg |
| Dimensions, length × width × height | 160 × 78 × 76 cm |
| Electric motors | 2 × 4,000 W |
| Maximum speed | 3.5 km/h |
| Maximum payload | 500 kg |
| Water flow | Up to 3,000 L/min |

## Key terms

- **Teleoperation**: a person remotely controlling a machine.
- **Payload**: the carried load, distinct from the robot's own weight.
- **Thermal camera**: a camera producing images from infrared radiation associated with temperature.
- **Module**: an interchangeable assembly supplying a particular capability.

## Getting started

1. **Watch Shark Robotics' demonstration:** identify the human operator, tracks, and fitted mission tool before considering autonomy.
2. **Compare two configurations:** sketch the information and controls needed for a water cannon versus a stretcher carrier, without operating equipment.
3. **Read the technical table:** commercial price and student access are unknown; use this as a free systems-design case study.

> **Watch out:** Fire, pressurised water, and a heavy moving platform are genuine hazards; do not recreate a firefighting deployment for a student demo.

## Used in

- **Shark Robotics** develops Colossus with firefighter feedback; its modular tooling illustrates how one mobile base can support several emergency-response tasks.

lessons.name: DuaTorso
lessons.summary: DuaTorso is Duatic’s dual-arm robotic upper body, combining two DynaArms, vision, and coordinated control for mounting on a separate mobile platform.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

DuaTorso is Duatic’s dual-arm robotic upper body, combining two DynaArms, vision, and coordinated control for mounting on a separate mobile platform.

![Duatic’s published view of DuaTorso reaching toward a blue crate](/img/lessons/robots_robot-duatorso.webp)
*Duatic’s published view of DuaTorso reaching toward a blue crate. Source: [Duatic](https://www.duatic.com/duatorso), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A torso is not a complete mobile robot:** DuaTorso supplies the upper body; choosing and integrating a base remains a separate engineering decision.
- **Two arms can share a task:** Duatic combines its DynaArms with vision and coordinated whole-body control rather than selling two unrelated arm movements.
- **Modularity resembles software composition:** a reusable module exposes interfaces; its host still needs compatible power, mounting, and control.

> **Key idea:** Buying coordinated manipulation as a module moves the integration boundary; it does not remove that boundary.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **The central torso supports two arms:** the published image shows grippers beside a crate and a vision-equipped upper body, without a wheeled base.
- **ROS 2 is the communication interface:** it is robotics middleware for connecting software components; Duatic advertises native control and an open API.
- **An open API is not open hardware:** callable software interfaces do not establish permission to reproduce the robot or access to its complete design.
- **Peak and continuous payload differ:** the advertised 30 kg maximum applies for ten seconds, whereas the continuous rating is 12 kg.
- **A comparison example:** 30 divided by 12 is 2.5; the larger short-duration figure is not a promise of 2.5 times continuous lifting capability.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V["Vision"] --> C["Coordinated control"]
  A["ROS 2 commands"] --> C
  C --> T["Torso and two arms"]
  T --> O["Handle object"]
```

| DuaTorso specification | Manufacturer's value |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous payload | 12 kg |
| Maximum payload | 30 kg for 10 seconds |
| Reach per arm | 0.990 m |
| Degrees of freedom | 18 |
| Input power supply | 48 V DC |
| Total weight | To be determined |

## Key terms

- **Payload**: the load the robot handles, distinct from its own weight.
- **Degree of freedom**: an independently variable coordinate describing the mechanism's motion.
- **API**: the interface through which another program requests operations or reads data.
- **DC**: direct current, with a fixed electrical polarity rather than alternating polarity.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the bag-grasping demonstration:** it shows Duatic's integrated mobile system; distinguish the upper-body work from the base's movement.
2. **Write a free integration checklist:** list mechanical mounting, power, communication, and vision requirements before choosing a mobile base.
3. **Inspect the component driver repository:** its public code concerns DynaArm; do not assume it is a complete DuaTorso installation package.
4. **Check access before planning hardware work:** the product page publishes no price, and student access is unknown.

> **Watch out:** Powered arms and heavy loads create pinch and crush hazards; the payload comparison is not an instruction to test maximum lifting.

## Used in

- **Duatic** offers DuaTorso as the upper-body module alongside its integrated DXTR system; this is a manipulation component, not a walking humanoid.

lessons.name: EyeLib
lessons.summary: EyeLib is MIKAJAKI’s robotic eye-measurement station and associated software suite, combining optical measurements with patient information for clinician-facing reports.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EyeLib is MIKAJAKI’s robotic eye-measurement station and associated software suite, combining optical measurements with patient information for clinician-facing reports.

![EyeLib’s stationary white measurement unit with a blue viewing aperture and chin supports](/img/lessons/robots_robot-eyelib.webp)
*EyeLib’s stationary white measurement unit with a blue viewing aperture and chin supports. Source: [MIKAJAKI](https://mikajaki.ai/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Robotics can look like medical equipment:** EyeLib is a stationary measurement platform, not a walking assistant or a general-purpose arm.
- **Combining sensors is a systems problem:** the station gathers objective measurements while a separate virtual assistant collects symptoms and patient-reported information.
- **A report is not clinical proof:** vendor descriptions do not independently establish diagnostic accuracy or clinical efficacy.

> **Key idea:** Automating measurement and combining data are separate from establishing that a medical conclusion is correct.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **The station integrates optical instruments:** MIKAJAKI lists measurements of eye shape, dimensions, pressure, and internal structures within one platform.
- **OCT provides internal views:** optical coherence tomography uses light to image tissue layers, including the front and back of the eye.
- **Smartbot gathers subjective information:** patient answers and visual tests complement the physical station's measurements rather than replacing its instruments.
- **SmartVision presents combined results:** the software integrates measurements and patient information into an illustrated report for professional review.
- **Think of a typed data pipeline:** different instruments produce different fields; merging them into one record does not make those fields interchangeable.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Patient answers"] --> R["Combined report"]
  I["Optical instruments"] --> M["Eye measurements"]
  M --> R
  R --> C["Clinician review"]
```

| EyeLib Suite detail | Manufacturer's stated value |
| --- | --- |
| Station technologies | 10 |
| Optical/anatomical measurements | 100+, in the detailed station description |
| Advertised examination time | About 6 minutes |
| Station floor dimensions | 137 × 70 cm |
| Report display | 45 inches |

- **A timing example:** 60 divided by six gives ten slots per hour, excluding patient preparation, review, cleaning, and other workflow time.
- **Do not conflate timings:** the 2025 ESCRS submission describes six to ten minutes per patient; the current vendor page advertises about six.

## Key terms

- **Modality**: a distinct way of measuring or imaging something.
- **Objective data**: instrument measurements rather than the patient's description of symptoms.
- **Subjective data**: information reported by the patient, such as symptoms.
- **Triage**: directing patients toward appropriate follow-up according to assessed need.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the manufacturer's process video:** use this older demonstration to picture the patient station, not to verify current clinical performance.
2. **Make a free data-flow exercise:** create fictional fields for symptoms, measurements, and review status; keep each category separate.
3. **Compare the product and conference descriptions:** mark which statements describe hardware, workflow, or claimed medical outcomes.
4. **Treat access as professional:** price and student access are unknown; this lesson does not propose operating the medical system.

> **Watch out:** Do not collect patient data, perform eye examinations, or interpret disease risk as a student robotics exercise.

## Used in

- **MIKAJAKI** presents EyeLib for ophthalmology workflows; the engineering lesson is coordinated sensing and reporting with clinician review, not autonomous treatment.

lessons.name: Flinkbot
lessons.summary: Flinkbot is Flink Robotics’ full-size parcel-handling robot, combining an industrial arm, gripping hardware, and perception-driven control for singulation, loading, and unloading.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Flinkbot is Flink Robotics’ full-size parcel-handling robot, combining an industrial arm, gripping hardware, and perception-driven control for singulation, loading, and unloading.

![Flinkbot using suction cups to lift a cardboard parcel beside a conveyor](/img/lessons/robots_robot-flinkbot.webp)
*Flinkbot using suction cups to lift a cardboard parcel beside a conveyor. Source: [Flink Robotics](https://www.flink.so/product), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Logistics needs more than recognition:** robots must grasp mixed parcels and deliver them without collisions.
- **Singulation creates order:** the machine separates a messy bulk of parcels into an individual flow suitable for downstream sorting.
- **Distinguish the products:** Flinkbot mini targets smaller items and denser workstations; do not copy its specifications onto Flinkbot.

> **Key idea:** Warehouse automation succeeds when perception, gripping, movement, and the next conveyor all work as one system.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **An off-the-shelf arm provides motion:** Flink integrates its own gripping hardware and software around it.
- **Depth cameras inform a world model:** this is the software's working representation of objects, geometry, and contact in the current scene.
- **Suction cups can be controlled individually:** the vacuum gripper adapts which contact points engage the parcel surface.
- **Physics remains in the loop:** Flink says its model evaluates actions during deployment, not only training.
- **Think of an online scheduler:** changing inputs need updated decisions, not one fixed sequence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Depth cameras"] --> W["World model"]
  W --> A["Evaluate action"]
  A --> G["Arm and vacuum gripper"]
  G --> C
```

| Full-size Flinkbot specification | Vendor's product-table value |
| --- | --- |
| Base dimensions | 1 × 1 m |
| Footprint | 1 m² |
| Unit weight | Less than 300 kg |
| Handling weight | Up to 20 kg |
| Singulation rate | 1,400 parcels/hour |
| Loading/unloading/picking rate | 600–800 parcels/hour |

- **A throughput example:** 3,600 divided by 1,400 gives about 2.6 seconds per parcel on average, not a per-object guarantee.
- **Specifications are task-dependent:** the page's singulation narrative also mentions 35 kg; confirm the exact configuration rather than extending that figure to every Flinkbot task.

## Key terms

- **Singulation**: separating a bulk collection into individual items for the next process.
- **Gripper**: the tool that holds and releases an object.
- **World model**: an internal representation used to predict and plan physical interactions.
- **LIDAR**: distance sensing using laser light to monitor nearby space.

## Getting started

1. **Watch ETH Zürich's introduction:** track where parcels start and finish, not just whether the arm successfully lifts one.
2. **Calculate theoretical cycle time:** compare 1,400 parcels/hour with 800 parcels/hour to see why singulation and loading need separate performance figures.
3. **Map a free paper workflow:** draw incoming bulk, a pick zone, and a conveyor; locate possible grasp failures.
4. **Check commercial terms:** the vendor lists €12,000/month for its managed robot service and a €50,000 six-month trial; these differ, so request a quote.

> **Watch out:** Robot arms and moving parcels create crush hazards; LIDAR safety-zone claims do not justify entering an operating cell.

## Used in

- **Flink Robotics** targets roll-cage unloading, conveyor singulation, and outbound cage loading; student access is unknown.

lessons.name: Flinkbot mini
lessons.summary: Flinkbot mini is Flink Robotics’ compact handling system for picking small, varied items from dense bins, rather than the full-size robot’s parcel-handling workload.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Flinkbot mini is Flink Robotics’ compact handling system for picking small, varied items from dense bins, rather than the full-size robot’s parcel-handling workload.

![Flink Robotics’ published technical view of the compact Flinkbot mini arm and narrow wheeled base](/img/lessons/robots_robot-flinkbot-mini.webp)
*Flink Robotics’ published technical view of the compact Flinkbot mini arm and narrow wheeled base. Source: [Flink Robotics](https://www.flink.so/product), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Small items change the problem:** picking from crowded bins differs from unloading larger parcels.
- **High-mix means varied stock:** shapes, materials, and weights change rather than remaining identical.
- **Do not inherit sibling specifications:** Flinkbot mini has its own handling limit; Flinkbot's payload and singulation rate are not mini specifications.

> **Key idea:** A smaller robot is a different task-and-workspace package, not simply a full-size robot with the numbers scaled down.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A narrow base supports an articulated arm:** the manufacturer's technical view shows a compact platform on casters with a small suction tool.
- **Dense-bin picking is its stated role:** the product description emphasises rapid single-item picks across varied shapes and materials.
- **Shared intelligence tracks the scene:** Flink says every robot uses a sensor-derived world model to evaluate actions during operation.
- **Think of a crowded software interface:** selecting the intended target must not accidentally select its neighbour.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Sensors"] --> W["World model"]
  W --> P["Choose item and grasp"]
  P --> A["Arm and suction tool"]
  A --> S
```

| Flinkbot mini detail | Vendor's stated value |
| --- | --- |
| Base dimensions, product table | 1 × 0.4 m |
| Footprint, product table | 0.4 m² |
| Footprint, homepage | 0.5 m² |
| Unit weight | Less than 150 kg |
| Handling weight | Up to 10 kg |
| Dense-bin picking description | 1,000 picks/hour |

- **The footprint sources disagree:** keep both published values visible; required operating clearance is unknown, so neither figure alone establishes workstation fit.
- **A cycle-time example:** 3,600 seconds divided by 1,000 picks gives 3.6 seconds per pick, before interruptions.
- **Picking rates also differ:** the narrative says 1,000 picks/hour; the table lists 1,000–1,200 for loading, unloading, and picking. Neither establishes measured accuracy.

## Key terms

- **Footprint**: the floor area occupied by the unit, distinct from its entire movement or safety zone.
- **High-mix**: handling many different kinds of items rather than one standard part.
- **Pick-and-place**: grasping an item, transporting it, and releasing it at a destination.
- **Throughput**: completed items per unit time, which is not the same as success rate.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the official mini product view:** identify its narrow base and tool rather than substituting footage of the larger Flinkbot.
2. **Compare the two product columns:** record mini's handling limit, weight, and picking rate separately from Flinkbot and Flinkbot Duo.
3. **Try a free exercise:** arrange empty packages in a bin and list accessible surfaces; this does not reproduce Flink's planner.
4. **Resolve dimensions before procurement:** ask about operating clearance; a mini-specific quote and student access are unknown.

## Used in

- **Flink Robotics** positions Flinkbot mini for small, high-mix items in dense bins.

lessons.name: Furhat
lessons.summary: Furhat is a tabletop social robot with a projected animated face, a movable head, microphones, and a camera for building embodied conversational interactions.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Furhat is a tabletop social robot with a projected animated face, a movable head, microphones, and a camera for building embodied conversational interactions.

![Furhat’s white head-shaped face mask above its camera and speaker base](/img/lessons/robots_robot-furhat.webp)
*Furhat’s white head-shaped face mask above its camera and speaker base. Source: [Furhat Robotics](https://www.furhatrobotics.com/furhat-robot), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Conversation has a physical interface:** head direction, gaze, facial expression, and speech all affect how a person experiences an interaction.
- **A chatbot is one component:** choosing words does not coordinate gaze and motion.
- **Start without buying hardware:** the free software toolkit (SDK) includes Virtual Furhat for desktop prototyping; physical robot pricing is unknown.

> **Key idea:** An embodied conversation needs coordinated attention and timing, not merely a function that returns the next sentence.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A projector animates a shaped mask:** projected images change its appearance without mechanically moving facial features.
- **Three head axes create motion:** pan turns left/right, tilt looks up/down, and roll leans the head sideways.
- **Microphones and a camera provide input:** the robot has onboard audio sensing, an RGB camera, and a bundled external microphone array.
- **Software controls the interaction:** developers can build skills, send remote commands, or manually prototype responses through Wizard-of-Oz controls.
- **Think of an event-driven UI:** speech, gaze, and gestures respond to interaction events rather than one blocking text prompt.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U["Person speaks"] --> S["Speech input"]
  S --> K["Interaction software"]
  K --> R["Speech gaze and gesture"]
  R --> U
```

| Furhat platform specification | Manufacturer's value |
| --- | --- |
| Robot mass | 3.5 kg |
| Height × width × depth | 410 × 270 × 240 mm |
| Head motion | 3 degrees of freedom |
| Camera field of view | 120° diagonal |
| Projector resolution | 1,280 × 720 pixels |
| Bundled microphone array | 4 microphones |

- **A motion example:** the three axes allow turning, nodding, and leaning; this coordinate count does not describe conversational intelligence.
- **The virtual robot has limits:** current SDK documentation says camera-frame access is unavailable and streamed audio does not provide realtime lip movement there.

## Key terms

- **Back projection**: projecting an image onto a surface from behind it.
- **Skill**: a robot application defining an interaction or behaviour.
- **Wizard-of-Oz**: a person secretly or explicitly controlling responses while an interaction design is tested.
- **SDK**: a software development kit containing tools for building applications.

## Getting started

1. **Request the free SDK account:** follow the official launcher instructions rather than assuming the physical robot is required.
2. **Launch Virtual Furhat:** open its web interface and configure your microphone and audio output.
3. **Try speech, gaze, and a gesture:** use the documented controls to inspect these channels separately before combining them.
4. **Prototype one short exchange:** compare a greeting with and without coordinated gaze, keeping the words identical.

## Used in

- **Conversational & multimodal robot interfaces** connects spoken language to gaze and expression.
- **HRI foundations & user-study methods** helps turn an appealing demonstration into an explicit question about how people respond to the interface.

lessons.name: Gravis autonomous excavator retrofit kit
lessons.summary: Gravis turns existing excavators into supervised earthmoving robots using a rooftop computing kit, sensors, machine controls, and a tablet interface.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Gravis turns existing excavators into supervised earthmoving robots using a rooftop computing kit, sensors, machine controls, and a tablet interface.

![Gravis rooftop autonomy hardware on earthmoving equipment](/img/lessons/robots_robot-gravis.webp)
*Gravis rooftop autonomy hardware on earthmoving equipment. Source: [Gravis Robotics](https://www.gravisrobotics.com/rack), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Retrofit means adding capability:** the starting point is an existing excavator, not a robot designed from scratch.
- **Software meets hydraulics:** a digital command must ultimately move a heavy bucket through real soil.
- **Supervision is part of the product:** Slate supports in-cab assistance, field command, and remote operation rather than hiding the human interface.

> **Key idea:** An autonomy stack needs both a view of the terrain and a reliable way to command the original machine.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **RACK is the rooftop kit:** onboard computing processes camera and laser measurements, including when the machine is offline.
- **Smart masts combine sensors:** satellite-positioning antennas, cameras, and laser scanners help the system understand its surroundings.
- **Electronic valves connect commands to motion:** legacy machines may need an added electro-hydraulic valve before they can accept computer control.
- **Think of a device driver:** the planning software needs a machine-specific interface before its commands can affect physical hardware.

| RACK detail | Manufacturer's description |
| --- | --- |
| Supported machine mass | 10 to 100-plus tons |
| Terrain scanning | 360° LiDAR coverage |
| Supported equipment | Excavators and wheel loaders |
| Dump destinations | Spoil pile, hopper, or truck |
| Offline processing | Automotive-grade onboard computing |

## Key terms

- **LiDAR**: laser-based sensing used here to scan surrounding terrain in three dimensions.
- **GNSS RTK**: satellite positioning with corrections, used by the rear masts.
- **Electro-hydraulic interface**: electrically controlled valves that translate computer commands into hydraulic machine movement.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the explanation:** identify the original excavator separately from the added sensors and tablet.
2. **Compare machine coverage:** 100 divided by 10 gives a tenfold mass span, before the vendor's “plus”; this is not a digging-speed claim.
3. **Study the interfaces:** sketch sensor inputs, onboard computation, hydraulic commands, and operator stop as separate software boundaries.
4. **Request commercial access:** Gravis lists dealer rental and purchase routes; public kit pricing is unknown.

## Used in

- **Construction, quarry, and mining:** Gravis describes excavation and loading applications; the graph currently attaches no neighbouring project nodes.
- **Physical safety matters:** study the published workflow rather than experimenting on a working excavator; Slate includes an integrated wireless stop.

lessons.name: Inbolt GuideNOW
lessons.summary: Inbolt GuideNOW adds robot-mounted 3D vision and adaptive guidance so an industrial arm can locate parts and adjust its movements.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Inbolt GuideNOW adds robot-mounted 3D vision and adaptive guidance so an industrial arm can locate parts and adjust its movements.

![Inbolt industrial vision-guidance installation at Stellantis](/img/lessons/robots_robot-inbolt-guidenow.webp)
*Inbolt industrial vision-guidance installation at Stellantis. Source: [Inbolt](https://www.inbolt.com/product/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Seeing changes programming:** a part need not remain exactly where an earlier robot program expected it.
- **Integration beats a standalone detector:** the output must reach the robot controller quickly enough to change movement.
- **Names have evolved:** the graph calls this GuideNOW; the current manufacturer and UR listing describe Inbolt's wider intelligent vision-guidance platform.

> **Key idea:** Finding an object is useful only when its measured position can correct the robot's next movement.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A robot-mounted 3D camera measures the scene:** the listed package includes a camera, mount, controller, cables, and Inbolt Studio software.
- **CAD supplies the part description:** the system trains from computer-aided design models rather than requiring users to label image datasets.
- **Control software adapts motion:** the platform connects perception to supported industrial robot controllers, including Universal Robots.
- **Think of a feedback-driven API client:** new measurements update the next command instead of replaying a fixed request sequence.

| Published detail | Stated value or requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Platform localization accuracy | 0.5 mm |
| Platform perception-to-motion delay | Under 80 ms |
| UR software | PolyScope 5, version 5.13 or above |
| UR interface option | RTDE, included |
| Part references in one program, UR listing | Over 80 |

- **Keep timing claims separate:** the Vision Model page's under-2-ms pose updates are not the entire perception-to-motion delay.

## Key terms

- **Pose**: an object's position and orientation, both needed to guide a tool toward it.
- **Fixture**: hardware that holds a part in a repeatable location.
- **Trajectory**: the path the robot follows while carrying out an operation.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the product demonstration:** look for changes in part placement and the corresponding arm movement.
2. **Convert the timing:** 80 milliseconds equals 0.08 seconds; distinguish this platform figure from the vision model's internal update time.
3. **Check integration first:** compare your controller and software against the UR listing before proposing a lab installation.
4. **Request a demonstration:** this is commercial equipment; public pricing is unknown, and the linked documentation requires login.

## Used in

- **Inbolt** builds the system for applications including bin picking, fastening, de-racking, and gluing.
- **Moving industrial arms are hazardous:** a vision upgrade does not itself establish that a cell is safe for people.

lessons.name: Mori3
lessons.summary: Mori3 is an EPFL research robot whose triangular modules connect and change shape to form different moving, manipulating, and interactive structures.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Mori3 is an EPFL research robot whose triangular modules connect and change shape to form different moving, manipulating, and interactive structures.

![Mori3 triangular modules assembled into a reconfigurable structure](/img/lessons/robots_robot-mori3.webp)
*Mori3 triangular modules assembled into a reconfigurable structure. Source: [EPFL](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/mori3-a-polygon-shapeshifting-robot-for-space-tr-4/), CC BY-SA 4.0.*

## Why it matters for us

- **The body can be programmable:** different arrangements of the same modules support different functions instead of committing to one fixed robot shape.
- **Versatility has a trade-off:** EPFL explicitly notes that specialized robots can outperform this general-purpose approach on particular tasks.
- **Space travel motivates compactness:** the researchers envisage reusing modules where storing many dedicated robots would be difficult, not a demonstrated space deployment.

> **Key idea:** Reconfiguring the mechanism changes which tasks the same collection of robot modules can attempt.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Triangular modules are robots themselves:** each has power, motors, and sensors; alone, a module can drive and change its edge lengths.
- **Connected modules form articulated structures:** they attach, communicate, and coordinate to produce larger shapes and movements.
- **Local electronics handle the module:** the published code separates the main microcontroller, Wi-Fi firmware, external control, and experiment trajectories.
- **Think of composable software components:** the interfaces remain recognizable, but changing the connection graph changes what the whole system can do.

| Research implementation detail | Published value or component |
| --- | --- |
| Basic polygon | Triangle, 3 edges |
| Low-level controller | 16-bit dsPIC33EP512GM604 |
| Wireless chip | ESP8266EX |
| External control implementation | Python 3.6.6 |
| Experiment analysis environment | MATLAB 2020b |

- **These are historical implementation details:** the repository documents the research setup, not a promise of compatibility with a current student laptop.

## Key terms

- **Module**: one functional unit that can connect to others.
- **Polygon meshing**: assembling polygonal pieces into a larger shape, physically here rather than only in computer graphics.
- **Morphology**: the robot's physical shape and arrangement of parts.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the transformations:** classify each demonstrated arrangement as locomotion, manipulation, or interaction.
2. **Count a simple arrangement:** two separate triangles have six edges in total; joining an edge pair creates one connection between modules.
3. **Inspect the repository:** trace external commands toward the module controller without assuming you can run hardware-dependent code on its own.
4. **Start with paper triangles:** explore connection graphs for free; hardware purchase price and student access are unknown.

## Used in

- **EPFL Reconfigurable Robotics Lab (RRL)** developed Mori3 as a research demonstration of physical polygon meshing.
- **Experiment code is public:** the repository includes trajectories and figure-generation data; public code is not evidence of a purchasable robot kit.

lessons.name: Open Duck Mini v2
lessons.summary: Open Duck Mini v2 is an open-source miniature biped inspired by Disney’s BDX droid, with printable parts and learned walking policies.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Open Duck Mini v2 is an open-source miniature biped inspired by Disney’s BDX droid, with printable parts and learned walking policies.

![Community-built Open Duck Mini v2 robots pictured in the project README](/img/lessons/robots_robot-open-duck-mini-v2.webp)
*Community-built Open Duck Mini v2 robots pictured in the project README. Source: [Open Duck Mini](https://github.com/apirrone/Open_Duck_Mini), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A small body still needs integration:** mechanical assembly, electronics, calibration, and software must agree before a walking policy can help.
- **The project exposes the whole pipeline:** separate repositories cover the physical design, simulation training, and onboard execution.
- **Do not confuse inspiration with manufacturer:** contributors are making a miniature BDX-inspired robot; this is not Disney's original hardware.

> **Key idea:** A downloadable walking policy becomes useful only when the real robot's configuration matches what that policy expects.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Printed parts form the body and legs:** the print guide distinguishes ordinary PLA parts from flexible TPU foot components.
- **An onboard Raspberry Pi runs the runtime:** setup includes checking motors, testing the motion sensor, and recording joint offsets.
- **Training happens separately:** Open Duck Playground contains MuJoCo environments and exports policies for inference, meaning running a trained model.
- **Think of a compiled application:** training produces an artifact, but runtime dependencies and machine configuration still determine whether it behaves correctly.

| Project detail | Source-stated value |
| --- | --- |
| Height, legs extended | About 42 cm |
| Full bill-of-materials target | Under US$400 |
| Documented onboard computer | Raspberry Pi Zero 2W |
| Standard PLA print infill | 15% |
| TPU foot-bottom infill | 40% |

- **Budget is a target, not a quote:** the README's parts estimate does not establish a delivered French lab cost.

## Key terms

- **Policy**: the trained model used to choose the robot's actions.
- **Sim-to-real**: transferring behaviour developed in simulation onto physical hardware.
- **Joint offset**: a calibration correction aligning a motor reading with the intended physical joint position.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the README's Duck1.mp4:** identify balancing and recovery behaviour before considering a physical build.
2. **Compare print settings:** 40 minus 15 gives 25 percentage points more infill for the TPU foot bottom, not a universal strength guarantee.
3. **Start in simulation:** inspect Playground's Open Duck Mini v2 inference example; the source code is freely accessible before buying parts.
4. **Follow runtime calibration:** test the IMU and motors, then set joint offsets before attempting the documented walking workflow.

## Used in

- **Open Duck Mini build** is the map's corresponding student project.
- **Smart servos & serial actuator buses** and **Open-source actuator & electronics stacks for legged/humanoid robots** provide supporting integration knowledge.
- **Avoid experimental head control:** the runtime README explicitly warns that it can break the robot's head.

lessons.name: Pathfinder
lessons.summary: Pathfinder is ACWA Robotics’ autonomous pipe-inspection robot, designed to collect condition and location data inside operating water-distribution networks.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Pathfinder is ACWA Robotics’ autonomous pipe-inspection robot, designed to collect condition and location data inside operating water-distribution networks.

![Pathfinder pipe-inspection robot in ACWA Robotics’ official image gallery](/img/lessons/robots_robot-pathfinder.webp)
*Pathfinder pipe-inspection robot in ACWA Robotics’ official image gallery. Source: [ACWA Robotics](https://www.acwa-robotics.com/images-gallery/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **The deliverable is useful data:** a pipe operator needs to know where damage is, not merely that a robot completed a trip.
- **The environment changes the design:** the machine must travel through pipes, bends, and flowing water while carrying inspection sensors.
- **Navigation cannot assume satellite reception:** ACWA describes Canaloc as GPS-free positioning that combines multiple data sources.

> **Key idea:** Inspection measurements need a location attached to them before they can guide maintenance decisions.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A mobile sensor platform follows a programmed mission:** Pathfinder can travel in or against the flow and negotiate elbows and branches.
- **Sensors match the pipeline:** the selected material and diameter affect which measurements are collected, including imagery and residual wall thickness.
- **Canaloc reconstructs the route:** measurements and images are associated with the path travelled during inspection.
- **Think of structured application logs:** a warning without a timestamp or request identifier is much harder to investigate; pipe defects similarly need context.

| Reported field example | Published conditions |
| --- | --- |
| Bordeaux pipe diameter | 250 mm |
| Bordeaux round-trip mission | 400 m |
| Bordeaux pressure | 3–5 bar |
| Marseille pipe diameter | 400 mm |
| Marseille inspected length | More than 1 km |

- **These are mission examples:** they are not universal maximum diameter, range, or pressure specifications for every Pathfinder configuration.

## Key terms

- **Residual thickness**: the pipe-wall material remaining, used to assess its condition.
- **Digital twin**: a digital representation of the inspected network and associated data.
- **GIS**: a geographic information system that can combine mapped infrastructure with inspection results.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the ACWA case-study video:** connect the robot's physical constraints to its engineering workflow before reading the field reports.
2. **Interpret the Bordeaux distance:** a 400-metre round trip would mean 200 metres outbound if the return followed exactly the same route.
3. **Make a free data mock-up:** attach a pipe-segment identifier, distance, image, and defect label to each fictional inspection record.
4. **Contact ACWA for access:** public purchase pricing is unknown; this is a professional inspection solution, not a documented student assembly kit.

## Used in

- **ACWA Robotics** reports missions for water utilities, including Bordeaux and Marseille, collecting evidence for infrastructure management.
- **Drinking-water access is controlled:** ACWA specifies a sanitized airlock; do not put a student prototype into an operating public water network.

lessons.name: rc_visard NG
lessons.summary: rc_visard NG is a stereo vision sensor with onboard computing that gives industrial robots depth images and task-specific information such as grasp points.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

rc_visard NG is a stereo vision sensor with onboard computing that gives industrial robots depth images and task-specific information such as grasp points.

![The rc_visard NG sensor and its physical components](/img/lessons/robots_robot-rc-visard-ng.webp)
*The rc_visard NG sensor and its physical components. Source: [Roboception](https://doc.rc-visard-ng.com/latest/en/hardware_spec.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Vision becomes a service:** the sensor combines image capture and processing instead of sending every computation to a separate desktop.
- **Integration is familiar:** its web interface and REST API connect industrial perception to skills we already use in software projects.

> **Key idea:** A useful robot camera must deliver actionable geometry, not just attractive pictures.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Two cameras see one scene:** stereo matching compares their views to estimate depth, or distance from the sensor.
- **Onboard computing runs perception:** optional rc_reason modules provide information such as grasp points; available modules depend on the installation.
- **UserSpace runs custom software:** Docker containers let developers add application logic directly on the sensor, like deploying another service beside an API.
- **Do not mix model specifications:** the table describes the manual's monochrome 160-6 configuration, not every newer hardware option.

| Manual: rc_visard NG 160-6 | Specification |
| --- | --- |
| Camera resolution | 1440 × 1080 pixels, monochrome |
| Stereo baseline | 160 mm |
| Compute | Orin Nano 8 GB |
| Supply voltage | 18–30 V |
| Mass | 0.965 kg |
| Cooling | Passive |

## Key terms

- **Baseline**: distance between the two cameras; here 160 mm means 16 cm.
- **Point cloud**: a collection of three-dimensional points representing the visible scene.
- **Confidence image**: a per-pixel quality measure accompanying the estimated depth, useful when deciding which measurements to trust.

## Getting started

1. **Start free:** read the manual and watch the metal-parts demonstration; hardware is commercial and its price is unknown here.
2. **With authorized hardware:** open the sensor's IP address in a browser and inspect the Camera and Depth Image pages.
3. **Export a snapshot:** compare camera images, depth, and confidence before attempting any arm integration; snapshots can affect running acquisitions.

## Used in

- **Roboception** supplies the platform; its published demonstration uses rc_visard NG and CADMatch to place metal parts in a tray.
- **Keep motion separate:** testing perception does not require enabling a live industrial robot arm.

lessons.name: Reachy Mini
lessons.summary: Reachy Mini is a programmable desktop robot with an expressive moving head and antennas for experimenting with human–robot interaction and AI applications.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Reachy Mini is a programmable desktop robot with an expressive moving head and antennas for experimenting with human–robot interaction and AI applications.

![Reachy Mini expressing itself with its head and antennas](/img/lessons/robots_robot-reachy-mini.webp)
*Reachy Mini expressing itself with its head and antennas. Source: [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/blog/reachy-mini), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A desk-sized interface:** Python code can control physical expression rather than only drawing a chatbot response on a screen.
- **Try before buying:** the SDK includes simulation, so the first learning exercise does not require ordering a kit.

> **Key idea:** A robot interaction includes timing and movement, not only the words produced by a language model.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Head and body move:** the head has six degrees of freedom; the body rotates and two antennas add expressive cues.
- **Camera and microphones provide input:** applications choose how to use their signals; connecting an AI model is an application decision.
- **Python exposes behaviours:** think of the robot as an API with a physical output device instead of a web page.
- **Separate versions:** current docs distinguish Wireless with onboard Raspberry Pi CM4 computing from Lite, which runs on your computer.

| Published launch specifications | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Height | Approximately 28 cm |
| Width | Approximately 16 cm |
| Mass | 1.5 kg |
| Head motion | 6 degrees of freedom |
| Animated antennas | 2 |
| Launch prices | Lite US$399; Wireless US$499, before tax/shipping |

## Key terms

- **Degree of freedom**: an independent motion coordinate, not a count of conversational skills.
- **SDK**: the software development kit used to write and test robot applications.
- **Onboard compute**: a computer inside the robot rather than a separate laptop.

## Getting started

1. **Start free in simulation:** follow the current SDK guide before choosing Lite or Wireless hardware; verify current prices before ordering.
2. **Run a small movement:** the documented example combines a 10 mm head offset and 15° roll over one second.
3. **Add one input:** connect a simple camera or speech interaction only after understanding movement limits and data handling.

## Used in

- **Reachy Mini custom expressive behaviours on the edge** and **Voice-commanded Reachy Mini** are corresponding map projects.
- **Interruptible conversational robot** and **Socially assistive coach robot** are related project proposals, not claims of validated medical capabilities.
- **Embedded Linux & companion computers**, **Edge AI hardware & on-device inference**, and **Hugging Face (LeRobot)** supply neighbouring map context.

lessons.name: RoBoa confined-space robot
lessons.summary: RoBoa is a soft, growing robot that extends a fabric tube into confined spaces for inspection and task-specific work.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

RoBoa is a soft, growing robot that extends a fabric tube into confined spaces for inspection and task-specific work.

![RoBoa soft tube and head in a confined-space application](/img/lessons/robots_robot-roboa.webp)
*RoBoa soft tube and head in a confined-space application. Source: [RoBoa](https://www.roboa.ch/solution), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Access shapes the design:** wheels are not the only answer when the route is narrow, winding, or difficult to reach.
- **Software meets a soft body:** this platform makes the physical mechanism as important to the mission as the control interface.

> **Key idea:** Growing forward from a tube can reach places where dragging an entire rigid robot would be difficult.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **The base handles control:** RoBoa describes it as the module for control, autonomy, and communication, separate from the body and sensor head.
- **The tube everts:** fabric turns outward as the robot extends, rather than propelling a conventional wheeled chassis down the route.
- **Compressed air drives growth:** ETH describes a soft pneumatic architecture; pneumatic means operated using pressurized air.
- **Heads change the task:** modular sensors and tools support inspection or installation. Think of the head as a plugin behind a shared interface.

| Published platform detail | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Extension reported by ETH in 2024 | Up to 100 m |
| Body | Replaceable textile tube |
| Main modules | Base, tube, head |
| Propulsion | Pneumatic growth by eversion |
| Rescue communication equipment | Speaker and microphone |

## Key terms

- **Eversion**: turning the tube outward to extend the robot into its surroundings.
- **Pneumatics**: using compressed air to produce movement rather than relying on wheels for traction.
- **Modularity**: changing a task-specific component without replacing the whole platform.

## Getting started

1. **Start free with the demonstration:** trace which parts remain outside the opening and which parts advance through it.
2. **Separate evidence from promises:** the 100 m figure is ETH's reported capability, not a guarantee for every pipe geometry or payload.
3. **Plan an inspection exercise on paper:** list the images, diagnostics, and operator decisions needed; commercial hardware price and student access are unknown.

## Used in

- **RoBoa** is the neighbouring builder node; its current site describes industrial piping, infrastructure, and cable-installation applications.
- **Rescue remains an application track:** the current rescue page invites pilots and labels the offering coming soon, rather than documenting routine deployment.
- **Do not enter live infrastructure:** use published demonstrations instead of experimenting in operational pipes or unstable rubble.

lessons.name: Swan
lessons.summary: Swan is SquareMind’s robotic skin-imaging system, combining automated full-body dermoscopy with software that supports comparison between patient visits.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Swan is SquareMind’s robotic skin-imaging system, combining automated full-body dermoscopy with software that supports comparison between patient visits.

![SquareMind Swan robotic skin-imaging system](/img/lessons/robots_robot-swan.webp)
*SquareMind Swan robotic skin-imaging system. Source: [SquareMind](https://www.squaremind.com/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Perception needs repeatability:** a useful medical image collection must support comparisons, not merely produce a visually impressive scan.
- **Robotics supports a workflow:** this example connects motion planning, imaging, storage, and image review instead of treating AI as a standalone answer.

> **Key idea:** Automating image acquisition and detecting change are different jobs from making a clinical diagnosis.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **A robotic imaging system maps skin:** SquareMind describes automated full-body dermoscopy completed in minutes, without publishing an exact duration on its landing page.
- **Software coordinates acquisition:** the EU project report explicitly lists robotic planning and control, imaging, time optimization, and secure storage.
- **AI compares visits:** the reported software detects new or modified moles; that is a change-detection task, not proof that every change is cancer.
- **Think of a version diff:** comparing two image collections can highlight what changed, but a highlighted difference still needs interpretation.

| Published system detail | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Imaging coverage | Full or partial body |
| Image detail | Dermoscopic definition |
| Acquisition | Automated, in a few minutes |
| Comparison target | New or modified moles between visits |
| Software work reported | Planning, control, imaging, secure storage |

## Key terms

- **Dermoscopy**: close examination of skin with a dermatoscope; Swan aims to extend that imaging detail over the body.
- **Change detection**: identifying differences between observations taken at different times, rather than assigning a diagnosis from a single picture.
- **Motion planning**: choosing how the robot should move while gathering the intended image collection.

## Getting started

1. **Start free with the official video:** identify the moving hardware, the person being imaged, and the software output as separate components.
2. **Read the EU report:** distinguish what the project reports achieving from what the product landing page promises; public hardware pricing is unknown.
3. **Sketch a nonclinical software exercise:** represent two visits as image collections, then define how a reviewer would inspect candidate differences.

## Used in

- **SquareMind** is the actual neighbouring map node and the company behind Swan; the graph lists no neighbouring student project.
- **Keep exercises nonclinical:** do not use a student comparison prototype to diagnose skin lesions or handle identifiable patient photographs.

lessons.name: Tribot
lessons.summary: Tribot is EPFL’s folding, insect-inspired research robot, able to switch movement modes and cooperate with other Tribots.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Tribot is EPFL’s folding, insect-inspired research robot, able to switch movement modes and cooperate with other Tribots.

![Tribots and a jumping Tribot photographed by Zhenishbek Zhakypov](/img/lessons/robots_robot-tribot.webp)
*Tribots and a jumping Tribot photographed by Zhenishbek Zhakypov. Source: [EPFL](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/robot-ants-that-can-jump-communicate-and-work-toge/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Mechanics can simplify software:** a folding body and specialized actuators provide several movement modes without a conventional wheeled drive.
- **Coordination creates capability:** the research demonstrates small robots sharing roles and moving objects together, rather than making each robot individually powerful.

> **Key idea:** A team can solve a task by dividing sensing, communication, and physical work between simple members.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Folded layers form three legs:** thin mechanical, material, and electronic layers become a T-shaped origami structure.
- **Shape-memory alloy actuators:** these materials change shape with temperature, driving crawling and stored-energy jumping mechanisms.
- **Sensors support teamwork:** infrared communication and proximity sensing let robots detect obstacles and exchange information without relying on GPS.
- **Think of distributed workers:** explorers find obstacles, a leader coordinates, and workers combine their effort; roles can change with the mission.

| 2019 untethered research version | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass | 10 g |
| Legs | 3 |
| Locomotion modes | 5 |
| Power | Onboard battery |
| Sensing and communication | Proximity and infrared |
| Vertical jump reported by IEEE | 14 cm |

## Key terms

- **Gait**: a movement pattern; Tribot can jump vertically, jump horizontally, somersault, walk, or crawl.
- **Untethered**: operating without an external power cable; earlier Tribot versions differed, so do not combine their specifications.
- **Shape-memory alloy**: a metal that recovers a shape when heated, used here as an actuator rather than a conventional motor.

## Getting started

1. **Start free with EPFL’s video:** identify the five movement modes and note which obstacle each addresses.
2. **Trace the cooperation example:** IEEE describes five robots: one leader, two workers, one monitor, and one messenger; 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5.
3. **Simulate messages, not mechanics:** write a small role-assignment exercise before considering fabrication; public kit pricing and student hardware access are unknown.

## Used in

- **EPFL Reconfigurable Robotics Lab (RRL)** is the neighbouring laboratory node and publishes Tribot’s research history.
- **Rescue is prospective:** the EPFL article suggests future search missions; the demonstrated collective behaviours are not evidence of field rescue deployment.
